events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Grand Theft Auto V Released
events.blurb: A crime game set in a fictionalised Los Angeles earned $800 million on its first day and $1 billion within three days — the fastest any entertainment product in history had reached that figure at that time. Guinness certified six world records on launch day. More than a decade later it continues to generate revenue through its online component.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 2013 — GTA V launched for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. It broke six Guinness World Records including fastest entertainment property to gross $1 billion. The game has sold over 200 million copies. GTA Online continues to generate over $1 billion annually.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya Founds the Mauryan Empire
events.blurb: A young commander, advised by the strategist Chanakya, overthrew the last Nanda king of Magadha and seized the throne of Pataliputra. He then turned west to fill the power vacuum left by a retreating Macedonian army, consolidating the first empire to rule most of the Indian subcontinent under a single administration — complete with a spy network, standardized taxation, and a standing army of 600,000.
events.revealBlurb: c. 322 BCE — Chandragupta Maurya, guided by Chanakya, whose political treatise the Arthashastra is basically ancient India's "The Prince" — except sharper, and with chapters on crocodile moats.

events.title: Harihara and Bukka Found the Vijayanagara Empire
events.blurb: Two brothers from a family of provincial commanders — who had previously served both the Kakatiya and the Delhi Sultanate before being captured, converted, and then reportedly re-converted to Hinduism — established a new kingdom on the south bank of the Tungabhadra river. The city they built, Vijayanagara ("City of Victory"), grew into one of the largest in the medieval world, shielding South India's temple culture from northern incursions for two and a half centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1336 CE — Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, Tungabhadra river, Karnataka. Today their capital is called Hampi — a UNESCO World Heritage Site of 1,600 monuments sprawled over 26 square kilometres of boulder-strewn landscape. Monkeys included at no extra charge.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Lands at Calicut
events.blurb: A Portuguese fleet rounded the tip of Africa and crossed the Indian Ocean, arriving at the most important spice port on the Malabar Coast. The Zamorin of Calicut received the visitors politely until he saw their gifts — cheap cloth and coral beads — and dismissed them. But the sea route was now open. Within decades, Portuguese cannon fire would dominate Indian Ocean trade routes that Arab, Persian, and Indian merchants had controlled for a thousand years.
events.revealBlurb: 20 May 1498 CE — Kozhikode (Calicut), Kerala. Da Gama's route around Africa was guided partly by an Indian navigator, Ahmad ibn Majid, who he reportedly bribed in Malindi. The pepper and spices he brought back to Lisbon were worth 60 times the voyage's cost.

events.title: Akbar Secures the Mughal Throne
events.blurb: A 13-year-old Mughal prince was crowned emperor at Kalanaur, Punjab, moments after his father fell down a library staircase in Delhi. His regent Bairam Khan immediately faced a formidable rival — the Hindu general Hemu, who had taken Delhi with 30,000 cavalry and 1,500 war elephants. At the second Battle of Panipat, Hemu was felled by a stray arrow mid-battle, his army collapsed, and the boy king's empire was saved.
events.revealBlurb: February 1556 CE — Akbar the Great. The same king who would later abolish the jizya tax, marry Rajput princesses, invent a syncretic religion, and reportedly have three thousand women in his harem started his reign as a frightened teenager hiding behind his general.

events.title: Guru Arjan Dev Is Executed by Mughal Order
events.blurb: The fifth Sikh Guru, who had compiled the Adi Granth and built the Golden Temple, was arrested by the Mughal emperor on charges of blessing a rebel prince. Ordered to pay a fine of 200,000 rupees and alter his scripture's hymns, he refused both. He was then tortured over several days — made to sit on a burning iron plate while red-hot sand was poured over his body — and died in Lahore. His execution permanently changed the relationship between the Sikh Panth and Mughal power.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1606 CE — Guru Arjan Dev Ji, Lahore, Mughal Empire under Jahangir. His martyrdom led his successor, Guru Hargobind, to take up two swords — one of spiritual authority, one of temporal power — and build an armed Sikh army.

events.title: Standard of Ur
events.blurb: Craftsmen in a wealthy Sumerian city-state inlaid a hollow wooden box the size of a laptop with lapis lazuli, red limestone, and shell to depict scenes of war on one side and peace on the other, reading top to bottom like a graphic novel. It was buried in a royal tomb and rediscovered only in 1927. Its original function is still debated — a musical instrument's soundbox, perhaps, or a processional standard.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2600 BCE — excavated by Leonard Woolley at the Royal Cemetery of Ur in modern Iraq. Now in the British Museum. Each inlaid figure is made of hundreds of pieces no larger than a fingernail.

events.title: Dürer's Self-Portrait
events.blurb: A 28-year-old German painter and printmaker completed a small panel depicting himself facing the viewer head-on, with long centre-parted hair and his right hand raised in a gesture traditionally reserved for depictions of Christ. It was a provocative piece of self-fashioning — the artist as holy creator. The inscription beside his head, dated to the year, pointed out how few European painters had ever signed their own faces.
events.revealBlurb: 1500 — Albrecht Dürer. Now in Munich's Alte Pinakothek. Dürer's German contemporaries thought the pose bordered on blasphemous. The picture has been read as the first true self-portrait-as-self-expression in Western art.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Velázquez's Las Meninas
events.blurb: A court painter completed a 3.2-metre oil depicting a 5-year-old Spanish princess surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting, two dwarfs, a dog, and — impossibly — himself at his easel. A distant mirror on the back wall reflects the figures of her parents, the king and queen, who appear to be standing exactly where the viewer stands. The painting is essentially a visual puzzle about who is depicting whom and from where.
events.revealBlurb: 1656 — Diego Velázquez at the Spanish court. The princess is Margarita Teresa. Now in Madrid's Prado. Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957. Foucault opened his book The Order of Things with a long reading of its perspective.

events.title: Van Gogh Cuts Off His Ear
events.blurb: After a violent argument with a fellow painter who had been living with him at a small yellow house in Provence for nine weeks, a 35-year-old Dutch artist cut off part of his own left ear with a razor, wrapped it in newspaper, and walked through the rain to deliver the package to a woman at a nearby brothel. He spent the night lying in a pool of blood. The fellow painter left the next morning. The injured man was committed to an asylum.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1888 — Vincent van Gogh; the houseguest was Paul Gauguin. He painted "Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear" within weeks. He sold only one painting in his lifetime and shot himself 19 months later in a Paris suburb.

events.title: NAACP Founded
events.blurb: A biracial group of activists, scholars, and newspaper editors met at a New York conference on the centennial of Abraham Lincoln's birth to establish an organization dedicated to fighting racial discrimination through legal action and public advocacy. W.E.B. Du Bois, the Harvard-trained sociologist, edited its magazine The Crisis; its lawyers would eventually argue Brown v. Board of Education.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1909 — National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It was founded partly in response to the Springfield, Illinois race riot the year before. Du Bois served as editor of The Crisis for 24 years.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street." Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: Executive Order 8802
events.blurb: Facing a threatened mass march on Washington organized by a prominent Black labor leader, a U.S. president signed an executive order banning racial discrimination in the defense industry and federal government. It was the first federal action against employment discrimination since Reconstruction. The threatened march was called off; the larger March would come 22 years later.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1941 — Franklin Roosevelt, pushed by A. Philip Randolph. Randolph had assembled 100,000 marchers and refused to call it off without the order. The order created the Fair Employment Practice Committee — a template for later civil rights enforcement.

events.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964 Signed
events.blurb: President Lyndon Johnson signed the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction, outlawing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in employment and public accommodations — ending the legal architecture of Jim Crow segregation. The bill passed after the longest Senate filibuster in history: 57 days.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1964 — The White House. Johnson reportedly told an aide after signing the bill, "We have lost the South for a generation" — a reference to the political realignment he expected. Johnson signed the bill with 75 ceremonial pens, handing them to civil rights leaders and the bill's sponsors.

events.title: George Floyd Murdered
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Black man was killed in a Midwestern American city when a white police officer kneeled on his neck for 9 minutes and 29 seconds while he was handcuffed face-down on the pavement. A 17-year-old bystander filmed the entire encounter on her phone. The video triggered the largest protest movement in American history — 15 to 26 million people marched across all 50 states over the following weeks.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 2020 — Minneapolis, officer Derek Chauvin. The bystander was Darnella Frazier; she received a Pulitzer Prize special citation. Chauvin was convicted of second-degree murder 11 months later and sentenced to 22 years. Protests spread to more than 60 countries.

events.title: Marco Polo Bridge Incident
events.blurb: A shot in the dark near an ancient stone bridge on the outskirts of a major northern city triggered a skirmish between two armies that had been eyeing each other for years. Within weeks, full-scale fighting had engulfed coastal metropolises hundreds of miles to the south, drawing in millions of troops and reshaping a continent.
events.revealBlurb: July 7, 1937 — the incident near Wanping that ignited the Second Sino-Japanese War. No one ever determined who fired first. Japan initially described it as a "local incident"; eight years later, roughly 35 million Chinese had died in the conflict it started.

events.title: Dunkirk Evacuation
events.blurb: Over nine days, 338,000 soldiers trapped against the sea by encircling armoured forces were lifted off a French beach by an improvised armada of naval destroyers, ferries, fishing boats, and private pleasure craft — while a rearguard held a tightening perimeter and aircraft fought overhead to keep the sky contested.
events.revealBlurb: May 26 – June 4, 1940 — Operation Dynamo. Planners hoped to save 45,000 men; they got 338,226. The "little ships" — about 700 civilian vessels ranging from lifeboats to Thames paddle steamers — became a national legend. Churchill warned Parliament not to call it a victory: "Wars are not won by evacuations."

events.title: Enigma Broken at Bletchley
events.blurb: A team of mathematicians and linguists working in a cluttered hut in the English countryside deployed an electromechanical machine that could test thousands of rotor settings per minute, cracking the daily-changed cipher used by an opposing military's command and logistics networks — and began reading intercepted messages within hours of their transmission.
events.revealBlurb: May 1940 — Bletchley Park's upgraded Bombe, designed by Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, began breaking Luftwaffe "Red" traffic daily. The secret was so tightly held that some commanders were fed cover stories about lucky reconnaissance flights. The intelligence was codenamed Ultra and arguably shortened the conflict by two years.

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: Battle of Okinawa
events.blurb: 180,000 American troops landed on an island 350 miles from the Japanese home islands on Easter Sunday, triggering the largest amphibious assault in the Pacific and the longest land battle of that theatre — 82 days of cave-to-cave fighting, mass suicide charges, and the heaviest naval losses the United States suffered in any single campaign.
events.revealBlurb: April 1 – June 22, 1945. US casualties: roughly 12,000 killed and 36,000 wounded. Japanese military deaths: over 110,000. An estimated 100,000 Okinawan civilians also died. The kamikaze campaign sank 36 US ships and damaged 368. American planners, projecting similar resistance during a home-island invasion, estimated 1 million US casualties — a figure that influenced the decision to use atomic bombs.

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Chrysler Building Completed
events.blurb: A 319-metre Manhattan skyscraper, topped with a radiator-cap-inspired sunburst spire, opened at the corner of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue as the tallest building in the world. Its automotive-magnate patron had kept the spire a construction secret; it was assembled inside the tower's upper levels and then hoisted into place in 90 minutes, triumphing over a rival bank project down Wall Street that had briefly claimed the height title. The Empire State Building eclipsed it 11 months later.
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1930 — architect William Van Alen for Walter Chrysler. The Art Deco ornamentation includes eagle gargoyles at the 61st floor and a 1,700-square-metre ceiling mural in the lobby. Van Alen was never paid his fee — Chrysler accused him of taking bribes from suppliers.

events.title: Golden Gate Bridge Opens
events.blurb: A 2,737-metre suspension bridge painted international orange opened across a strait connecting San Francisco Bay to the Pacific Ocean. At the time the longest suspension span in the world (1,280 metres between its towers), it had been built through the Depression with labour recruited off bread lines and union halls. Workers wore (then-innovative) hard hats and safety harnesses; a net slung below the deck saved 19 men who fell, dubbed the "Halfway to Hell Club."
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1937 — engineer Joseph Strauss, architect Irving Morrow. 200,000 people walked across on opening day. The famous "international orange" color is maintained by a full-time crew of 38 painters. Bridge suicides have been an anguishing running tally; a suicide barrier was finally completed in 2024.

events.title: Sydney Opera House Opens
events.blurb: A sail-shaped performing-arts complex on a harbour peninsula opened after 14 years of construction — ten times its original budget and nine years late. The Danish architect had won the design competition in 1957 but resigned in 1966 after political attacks and budget fights; he never saw the completed building. Its concrete "sails," covered in a million tiles of two shades of white, immediately made it one of the most recognized buildings in the world.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1973 — architect Jørn Utzon; opened by Queen Elizabeth II. Utzon was eventually reconciled with the building in 1999, 25 years after he left; he was awarded the Pritzker Prize in 2003 but never saw the interior of his own building. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: Turing's Computable Numbers
events.blurb: A 23-year-old British mathematician submitted a paper describing a hypothetical abstract machine — an infinite tape with a movable read/write head obeying a simple finite rule table — that could in principle compute anything a human mathematician could work out by following a procedure. The paper was intended to settle a famous open problem in formal logic; along the way it laid the mathematical groundwork for general-purpose computing.
events.revealBlurb: 1936 — Alan Turing, "On Computable Numbers." Written while he was a 23-year-old student. Turing worked with a physical analogue of the machine at Bletchley Park during WWII to break German Enigma ciphers. He was chemically castrated for homosexuality and died in 1954, probably by suicide.

events.title: First Cellular Phone Call
events.blurb: A Motorola engineer, standing on a Manhattan street with a 1.1-kilogram "brick" prototype handset to his ear, placed a phone call to his chief rival at a competing company's research lab — and made sure to inform him what he was doing. The handset's battery gave 35 minutes of talk time after 10 hours of charging. Motorola would spend another decade getting a lighter version to market.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1973 — Martin Cooper of Motorola called Joel Engel at Bell Labs. The prototype was the DynaTAC 8000x. It sold commercially in 1983 for $3,995. Cooper later said he'd been inspired by the communicator in Star Trek.

events.title: Ethernet Invented
events.blurb: An engineer at a Palo Alto research lab, inspired partly by a Hawaiian university's packet-radio network, drafted a memo describing a coaxial-cable local-area network that let multiple computers share a single transmission medium by listening before sending and backing off when collisions occurred. The protocol became the physical backbone of essentially every wired office and data-center network in the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1973 — Bob Metcalfe at Xerox PARC. He later co-founded 3Com to sell Ethernet products and became one of Silicon Valley's most quotable pundits. Metcalfe's Law — that a network's value grows with the square of its users — is named for him.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Joan of Arc Burned at the Stake
events.blurb: A 19-year-old French woman, captured by Burgundian allies of the English and sold to the English crown for 10,000 livres, was tried for heresy by a church court and burned to death in a market square of a Norman city. Her executioners dug through the embers to prove she had died rather than escaped. Her remains were thrown into the Seine. She was canonized by the Vatican 489 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1431 — Rouen. A retrial in 1456 cleared her of all charges. The principal heresy she had refused to recant was wearing men's clothes. She became a Catholic saint in 1920 — six years after French troops carried her image into the trenches of World War I.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Lunar Surface Landing
events.blurb: A spacecraft descended onto the Sea of Tranquility with 25 seconds of fuel remaining after the landing computer triggered five 1202 alarms caused by executive overflow. Two crew members spent 2 hours 31 minutes on the surface, collecting 21.5 kg of rock and soil and deploying a seismometer and a retroreflector array.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Apollo 11. Armstrong's first step came at 10:56 PM Eastern. The descent stage still sits on the Moon; the flag was knocked flat by the liftoff exhaust. The line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — the transmission dropped the article, and Armstrong spent decades insisting he said it.

events.title: Viking 1 First Mars Landing
events.blurb: NASA's Viking 1 lander touched down on Chryse Planitia, becoming the first spacecraft to successfully land on Mars and operate on its surface. Within minutes it returned the first color photographs of the Martian surface and began a biology experiment suite designed to detect signs of microbial life — whose results remain contested among planetary scientists.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1976 — Viking 1. The landing date was chosen deliberately: it was the seventh anniversary of the Apollo 11 Moon landing. Viking 1 operated for 2,245 Martian days — more than six Earth years — before its final transmission. One biology experiment produced an initially positive result for life that NASA later attributed to reactive soil chemistry.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Philae First Comet Landing
events.blurb: The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from the Rosetta orbiter and descended for seven hours to touch down on Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko, achieving the first landing on a comet in history. Philae's harpoon anchoring system failed on contact; the lander bounced twice across the surface over two hours before coming to rest in a shadowed crater.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 2014 — Rosetta/Philae. The comet is roughly the size of a city — about 4 km across — with gravity so weak that a person standing on it could jump to escape velocity. Philae's unplanned resting place in shadow left it unable to recharge its solar panels; it went silent after 57 hours. It sent one final signal in June 2015 before being confirmed lost.

events.title: First Commercial Crewed Orbital Launch
events.blurb: SpaceX Crew Dragon Endeavour launched two NASA astronauts to the International Space Station, marking the first crewed orbital launch from American soil since the Space Shuttle's retirement nine years earlier and the first time a commercially built and operated vehicle carried NASA astronauts to orbit. The spacecraft docked with the ISS approximately 19 hours after liftoff.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 2020 — Demo-2. The launch was originally scrubbed three days earlier at T-17 minutes due to a storm. Astronaut Doug Hurley — who had piloted the final Shuttle mission in 2011 — flew his second "last American launch from US soil" in nine years, except this time it wasn't the last. The touchscreen controls in the Dragon capsule replaced 800+ switches.

events.title: Spinning Jenny Invented
events.blurb: A Lancashire weaver, semi-literate and working out of his home, built a hand-cranked multi-spindle spinning frame that let one operator spin eight threads simultaneously rather than one. Later versions spun up to 120 spindles at once. Other weavers' wives in the district, seeing their cottage-industry spinning work disappearing, broke into his house and smashed his prototypes. He patented the invention six years later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1764 — James Hargreaves in Blackburn, England. Patented 1770. The name "Jenny" is probably derived from "gin," a contemporary term for a mechanical engine — not, contrary to popular story, after his daughter. Hargreaves died in poverty in 1778.

events.title: Morse Telegraph Demo
events.blurb: A 52-year-old former portrait painter sent the first message on a 61-kilometre experimental telegraph line between the US Supreme Court chamber and a Baltimore train station. The message, suggested by a friend's daughter, was a verse from the Book of Numbers. The demonstration proved the commercial viability of electrical long-distance communication; within a generation, telegraph cables had connected most of the inhabited world.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1844 — Samuel F. B. Morse. The message: "What hath God wrought!" Morse had spent years lobbying Congress for the line's $30,000 funding. He had only turned to the telegraph, in part, after failing to win a prestigious painting commission.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim. Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."
